messages.subject: GGIR: Wear time and sedentary time
messages.subject_clean: GGIR: Wear time and sedentary time
messages.body_plain:
Hello Vincent and fellow GGIR users,

I am a PhD candidate in Kinesiology, as well as a new GGIR and R user. The primary outcome of interest for my dissertation is sedentary behavior. I am using the GENEActiv to measure 30 consecutive days of sedentary behavior among an older adult population. I understand that there is some difficulty when distinguishing between postures using the current ENMO metric, but I am primarily interested in the ability of GGIR to detect sleep and non-wear time (as we did not collect sleep diaries from participants).

Typically, I restrict my analysis to participants that wore the accelerometer for at least 16 hours on at least three days per week over the 30-day period. Then, I look at the association between wear time and total sedentary time to see if I need to correct for the influence of variation in wear time. Therefore, I need to identify which variable represents total duration of wear time at the day level. Based on the data dictionary for part 5, I have identified non-wear time, but it is unclear which variable is duration of wear time at the day level. If possible, can you please direct me to the appropriate data output and variable needed to appropriately restrict participants based on wear time? Any feedback is appreciated.

Thank you!

Andrea

messages.subject: includedaycrit argument
messages.body_plain:
Hello Vincent and GGIR users,

One other item worth discussing is the includedaycrit argument. For part 2, we entered “16” as the minimum number of valid hours in day specific analysis. However, values for the “N valid hours” variable in the part2_daysummary csv file go below the specified 16 hour threshold. Similarly, the values for the “window_length_in_hours” variable in the part5_daysummary_MM_L50M100V400_T5A5 csv file go below the specified 16 hour threshold. Any thoughts on why this might be?

Thank you!

Andrea

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] late wakeup times in sleep detection
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] late wakeup times in sleep detection
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The GGIR release (v1.5-23) referenced in the Nature article is not available on git, do later versions of GGIR have this functionality?

Also, does the latest version of GGIR (v1.8-1) use the L5+/-6 method or the HDCZA method of sleep / wake detection when sleep logs are not used?

Thanks, Matt

On Monday, 14 January 2019 13:52:11 UTC-5, Vincent van Hees wrote:
> Hi Joan,
> Sorry for the late reply. Your finding seems to be in line with our paper from last year: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-31266-z. At a population level the method provides good estimates, but at an individual level measurement errors are expected.
>
> I did not design parameters for the algorithm to tweak the waking-up time earlier later. My proposal to address the problem would be:
>
> Do this only in the people for whom the waking up time ends after the breakfast time. Create a sleep diary (sleeplog, see GGIR documentation) where you use the breakfast time as wake-up time, and the currently estimates sleep onset time as sleep onset time.
> My expectation is that this will force the algorithm to avoid estimating waking-up time after breakfast.
>
> Further, it may be good to inspect the individual files and try to understand why the breakfast is included in the sleep period time window. For example, participant takes off the accelerometer after breakfast (e.g. during showering), participant goes back to bed after breakfast, or participant stops wearing the accelerometer because it is the last day of measurement.
>
> Best wishes,
> Vincent
>
> On Thu, 3 Jan 2019 at 17:11, <jo...@project-sapiens.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > We are using GGIR for a nutritional study and we found out that often (12% of cases) wakeup times are  approx 30 min later than participant's breakfast time.
> >
> > We are not using any sleep diary but the automated sleep period time window detection def.noc.sleep = c(1)
> >
> > Is there any parameter to tune the end of the sleeping period?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Joan
> >

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] GGIR: Wear time and sedentary time
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] GGIR: Wear time and sedentary time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrea,
You will probably be interested in the day specific variables: "nonwear_perc_day", "nonwear_perc_night", and "nonwear_perc_nightandday". Here, "perc" is my abbreviation for percentage.

Agree that metric ENMO will not inform you about postures. It is in the planning to expand GGIR with the sedentary sphere based classification of 'sitting behaviour (see papers by Alex Rowlands), possibly as optional sub-classes of what we currently call "inactivity" and "sustained inactivity bouts" in GGIR. This may be of value to you. Hopefully I can find time to do this later in the year. The essential signal metrics needed for this are already implemented, main outstanding task is to use them to make the classification.

As I quite often say in my responses to users: Support with the maintenance and development is always welcome. This can be either financially or in time commitment as motivated here: https://www.movementdata.nl/how-to-help-sustain-ggir.

Best wishes,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] includedaycrit argument
messages.body_plain:
If this happens then the values of the accelerometer derived variables (column O onward  in part2_daysummary.csv) should be blank.
This will enable you to spot which days are ignored and why.
For the person summary report (part2_summary.csv) those excluded are not used for calculating the averages.
However, please note that variables in "part2_summary.csv" that end with "_fullRecording" are derived from all data classified as "wear" (monitor worn) from all measurement days, including those excluded days. The motivation for these variables is that we try to use as much as possible for the data in the measurement classified as "wear" and apply a weighted average to handle the unbalanced nature of wearing a monitor over a day.

Vincent

Any feedback is appreciated.

Thank you,

Andrea
